Karen McNamara Australia is a generous and compassionate nation. Our society has been built upon a commitment to help those less fortunate and to look after our mates. Throughout the years Australia has had a strong social safety net for those in need. It is crucial that we ensure the sustainability of this safety net and guarantee that it will be there for generations to come. Over the past 12 months the federal government has spent approximately $150 billion on social services and welfare. This spending provides Australians with pensions, aged care, benefits to families and individuals, and the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Of this, the age pension is our largest welfare payment, totalling an estimated $44 billion in 2015-16. This represents close to 35 per cent of the Commonwealth budget. In the coming decade the costs of delivering these services will increase as our population grows and ages. The _Intergenerational_ _r__eport_ stated that the number of Australians aged 65 and over is projected to more than double by 2055. Future projections anticipate that by 2055 there will be approximately 40,000 people aged 100 and over. Payments made through age and service pensions are projected to increase each year, and in real monetary terms spending per person is projected to increase from almost $2,000 in 2014-15 to around $3,200 in 2054-55. Currently, this spending accounts for 2.9 per cent of our gross domestic product; without changes to how we deliver the age pension this amount will increase to 3.6 per cent of GDP by 2054-55. This is an unsustainable path for Australia. It is essential that we address the sustainability of Australia's pension system to ensure that we are able to provide for senior Australians in future years. The age pension provides support for 2.4 million Australians and contributes to a broad retirement income system, which also includes superannuation and voluntary savings. The majority agreed with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted in favour of reading the bill for a [second time](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that they can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill (as amended) makes changes to the assets test for all means tested income support payments, including allowances and pensions. Firstly, it increases the threshold above which your assests are tested (known as "free areas") for the purposes of support payments. In other words, people on allowances or full pensions can have more assets than they currently can before those assets are included in their means testing - but not that much more. See the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd129) for the asset test limits. People on allowances whose assets are above the free areas will no longer be eligible for that allowance while pensioners whose assets are above the free areas will have their pensions reduced at an increased rate. If someone is no longer eligible for a payment as a result of the changes, the bill makes them eligible for a concession card (either a Health Care Card or a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card). Read more in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd129).

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015, arguing it would cut pensions and break a promise, with 330,000 pensioners losing an average of $3,300 per year and 90,000 losing their pension entirely.

The government's proposed changes to the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015 will increase asset test thresholds, with single homeowners' threshold rising from $202,000 to $250,000 and couples' from $286,500 to $375,000, meaning 90% of pensioners will be better off or unchanged and 170,000 part-pensioners will move to full pension. The speaker criticised the opposition for lacking solutions and for opposing the bill, which also includes measures on defined benefit income, overseas pension payments, and automatic issuance of Commonwealth seniors health cards to those losing pension eligibility.

The speaker argued that Prime Minister Tony Abbott repeatedly promised no pension cuts before the 2013 election but now supports legislation cutting pensions for 330,000 low-income households and removing 90,000 entirely, calling the government untrustworthy and its deal with the Greens a broken promise.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015, arguing it would cut $2.43 billion from pensioners, with 330,000 worse off and 90,000 losing the part pension entirely. They detailed specific asset thresholds and income losses, accused the government of breaking pre-election promises, and criticised the Greens for supporting the bill.

The speaker argued against the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015, stating it would cut $2.4 billion from pensioners, with 91,000 losing their pension entirely and half of new retirees affected within 10 years. They proposed instead reducing superannuation tax concessions for high-income earners to save $14.3 billion over a decade, and said Labor would not support most measures but would back $1.5 billion in other savings.

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015 would refocus welfare toward those most in need by raising the assets test threshold for full pension eligibility and lowering the cut-out point, affecting 170,000 pensioners with an average $30 per fortnight increase. The bill was presented as necessary to address budget unsustainability blamed on the former Labor government, with the speaker stating the family home and superannuation would remain untouched under the coalition.

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015 is unfair, breaks a promise not to change pensions, and would cut incomes for low- and middle-income pensioners—single pensioners by up to $8,000 a year and couples by up to $14,000—by counting assets such as household contents, vehicles, and savings. They also defended Labor's past pension increases and criticized the government for targeting pensioners while avoiding revenue measures.

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015 will make 90% of Australia’s 3.7 million pensioners better off or unchanged, with 170,000 lower-asset constituents in the Lyne electorate gaining $30 a fortnight. Specific thresholds were cited: for full pension eligibility, the assets-free area rises to $250,000 for single homeowners and $375,000 for couple homeowners, while non-homeowners can have up to $699,000 in assets (couples) or $537,000 (singles) to be better off.

The speech opposed the government's pension bill, arguing it would cut pensions for 300,000 pensioners and remove them entirely for 90,000, with single pensioners holding $500,000 in assets losing about $8,000 and couples $14,000. It also criticised the coalition for freezing the superannuation guarantee at 9.5% until 2021 and allowing wealthy individuals—around 400 with over $10 million in super—to exploit tax concessions.

The Abbott government's Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015 attacks part-pensioners, breaking a pre-election promise of no pension cuts, and will leave over 300,000 pensioners worse off by doubling the asset test taper rate and abolishing the seniors supplement, pensioner education supplement, and education entry payment.

The speaker defended Labor's pension record, citing the Harmer review that delivered a $30 weekly increase for single pensioners, new indexation based on pensioner spending, and a rise in the indexation benchmark from 25% to 27% of male average weekly earnings, which reduced pensioner poverty from 27% to 12%. They criticised the Liberal Party for breaking a pre-election promise not to cut pensions, noting the 2014 budget proposed $23 billion in cuts amounting to $80 per week.

Labor will support the 10 per cent cap on defined benefit income and the abolition of the seniors supplement, but oppose the abolition of the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, reduced pension portability, and the asset-test taper changes, which the party says would leave nearly 330,000 part-pensioners $3,000–$5,000 a year worse off.

The bill breaks promises of no pension changes and no deals with the Greens, and will leave 327,300 current pensioners worse off, with 236,000 losing $130 per fortnight and 91,000 losing their pension entirely.

Labor opposed the bill, arguing it would cut pensions for 327,000 current part-pensioners, with singles losing up to $8,000 and couples up to $14,000, and 91,000 losing the pension entirely. They also criticised the government for promising no pension changes before the election and then pursuing cuts.

The speaker accused the Prime Minister of breaking a pre-election promise not to cut pensions, citing a previously proposed change to indexation that would have reduced pensioner incomes by up to $80 per week over 10 years. He argued the government’s actions demonstrate dishonesty and represent a "vicious attack" on Australian pensioners, contrasting Labor’s historical support for pensioners with the current government’s proposals.

The speaker argued for passing the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015, which denies part pensions to those with over $1 million in assets (excluding the family home) and increases full pensions by $30 per fortnight, and criticised Labor for opposing the reform while praising the Greens for their support.

The bill would cut the part pension for 330,000 part pensioners and affect another 700,000 workers nearing retirement, with examples given of a widowed teacher, a former dairy farmer, and a retired ambulance worker whose modest incomes would be reduced.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015, supporting Labor instead of the Coalition and Greens, citing a broken election promise, lack of grandfather provisions, and poor design that could strip pensioners of up to $8,000 annually and disincentivise saving.

The speaker argued that the government broke its pre-election promise not to change pensions, citing the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015. The speaker opposed the bill, citing analysis showing 80% of cuts affect low-income Australians, particularly single women, and gave the example of a constituent named Patricia who would lose $4,000 per year.

The speaker urged the government to provide consistency and stop changing pension rules, citing constituents’ difficulty in managing long-term affairs. They also requested advance notice of legislative changes to allow crossbenchers time to consult their communities before voting.

Mitch Fifield I was indicating to colleagues before the interruption that, under the Growing Jobs and Small Business package, there will be additional support options for young people with a mental illness, as well as young refugees and other vulnerable young migrants. There will also be a number of trials to provide intensive support to disadvantaged job seekers who have multiple barriers to work. These additional supports will be complemented by services through jobactive, which include work experience and better access to wage subsidies. But, most importantly, this measure will only apply to stream A job-ready individuals—that is, someone who resides in a labour market region, with good employment opportunities, and who has reasonable language, literacy and numeracy skills and recent work experience. A further 2015 budget measure in the bill will cease the Low Income Supplement from 1 July 2017. The measure will cease a supplement that has a very low take-up rate and is administratively highly complex. Indeed, service delivery costs in administering this payment far exceed the financial benefit accrued by the eligible individual. Many of those who qualify for the payment will continue to receive the energy supplement, with their family tax benefit payment. The bill also takes the opportunity to reintroduce some amendments relating to indexation that are currently before the Senate. The first of these indexation amendments will maintain at level for three years the income-free areas for all working-age allowances, other than student payments and parenting payment single. The start date for this was to have been 1 July 2015. The second amendment will maintain at level for three years the income-free areas and other means test thresholds for student payments, including the student income bank limits, with a new start date of 1 January 2016. They cited 54,000 affected youth, 20% youth unemployment in south-west Sydney, and cuts to Newstart and homelessness services, opposing the government's approach as cruel and economically harmful.

The speaker opposed the bill, arguing it would cut Newstart eligibility for 22–24 year olds from $519.20 to $426.80 per fortnight and impose a four-week waiting period with no income support, worsening already-high youth unemployment (14% nationally, 14.3% in Queensland) and citing $500 million in cuts to Indigenous programs.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Youth Employment and Other Measures) Bill 2015, which would impose a month-long waiting period for under-25 job seekers, raise the Newstart age from 22 to 24, and end the low-income supplement, citing 18.6% youth unemployment in the Hunter region and warning of financial hardship; they also announced $62,000 in emergency relief funding for Hunter storm-affected areas.

The speaker argued the bill would encourage young job seekers to find work by introducing a four-week waiting period for unemployment payments, with exemptions, and that it is part of a broader $375 million support package; he contrasted the coalition’s record of 280,000 jobs created and 300,000 fewer unemployed under the previous coalition government with Labor’s 200,000 increase in unemployment and 519,000 small business jobs lost.

The speaker argued for extending the waiting period for Youth Allowance for job seekers aged 16–25 to four weeks, and cited a meeting with Community Employers WA and VisAbility Guide Dogs WA, noting a KPMG cost-benefit analysis showing $5.58 of economic value per dollar invested in VisAbility’s employment program.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Youth Employment and Other Measures) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly denies young Australians income while employers like Baiada use 417 working holiday visas to bypass entry-level jobs, citing a Fair Work Ombudsman report that found Baiada obstructed investigations and used labour‑hire contractors with fabricated records.

This bill is part of a package that would tighten the rules for how unions and employer groups are run.
A new independent agency, the Registered Organisations Commission, would monitor these groups and have stronger powers to investigate and collect information.
The package would also create criminal penalties for officials who seriously breach their duties and raise financial transparency requirements.
Establishes the Registered Organisations Commission as an independent watchdog with enhanced investigation and information-gathering powers.
Adds new criminal offences and higher civil penalties for serious breaches of officers' duties.
Strengthens financial accounting, disclosure and transparency obligations by making certain rule requirements enforceable as civil remedy provisions.
Amends rules on officers' disclosure of material personal interests and changes disqualification and ineligibility grounds for office.

Brendan O'Connor No, the member for Gorton, Deputy Speaker Kelly. There is a member for O'Connor; I just do not happen to be the member for O'Connor. It is a magnificent story about a West Australian engineer who engineered the water pipeline to Kalgoorlie. He thought it had failed and he committed suicide. A week after that, the water arrived. That is why we got the member for O'Connor. My seat is named after a former Prime Minister, not a bad Prime Minister, John Grey Gorton. He was quite an interesting enigmatic sort of guy. I would prefer to be called the member for Gorton than the member for McMahon. Chris Bowen, a good colleague and friend of mine, I am sure would rather my title. I rise to remark upon the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2] before the House. This is, by the way, the third occasion that this matter has been before the House. For those of us who find the government's agenda to be a bit of a chaotic blur, albeit a nasty one, this is a bill that will establish the Registered Organisations Commission. The commission will be headed by a registered organisations commissioner with greater investigative power than those available to the general manager of the Fair Work Commission. The bill also modifies disclosure requirements, increases red tape and regulates individuals who choose, often on a voluntary basis, to dedicate their time to an employer body or union in the same way that the chief executives of corporate boards are also having to do. You could be forgiven for being a little confused that we are back in this place debating this bill because this is the third time those opposite have brought this bill forward. I will try not to be too cynical about politics but my generosity of spirit has been somewhat tried by the coalition's timing on this bill. In the primitive collective of those opposite, you can imagine it would have gone something like this: attack your rights at work with Work Choices, lose the election;

Christopher Back For clarity, colleagues, we now move to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No.2]. _A division having been called and the bells being rung—_ Richard Colbeck by leave—Mr President, I rise to make a point of clarification in respect of this division for people who were not in the chamber when I spoke just prior to the division being called. The government has given an assurance that this piece of legislation will not be called on today, in accordance with agreement between the opposition and the government. We understand that this piece of legislation is before a committee, and that committee should report to the parliament prior to it being considered. The basis of this division right now is that there is some concern that we may bring this on for debate today. I have made a statement to the chamber that that is not the case. It is the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014. It is before a committee and it should go through that process before it comes to the chamber. The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2] was reintroduced to enhance accountability and transparency of registered organisations by aligning obligations, penalties and regulator powers with the Corporations Act 2001, including increased civil penalties, new criminal offences for serious breaches, and the establishment of an independent Registered Organisations Commission within the Fair Work Ombudsman.

The speaker argued against the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2], stating it was a political attack on opponents rather than genuine reform, and noted that the previous Labor government had already strengthened transparency and penalties in 2012. He highlighted that employer bodies and unions both opposed the bill, and criticized Prime Minister Tony Abbott for using a royal commission to compel three Labor leaders (Kevin Rudd, Julia Gillard, Bill Shorten) to testify.

The government argued the bill would establish a Registered Organisations Commission to strengthen financial transparency, increase penalties, and introduce criminal offences for union misconduct, while denying claims of hostility toward unions and asserting the reforms would protect honest union members from corruption and scandal.

The speaker opposed the amendments to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2], arguing the bill is politically motivated to attack unions, not to improve governance. They cited the CFMEU’s exposure of a Liberal Party donor company underpaying temporary visa workers, which led to union investigations rather than employer penalties.

The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014, criticising union power and alleging corruption, and cited a 63% increase in shipping costs at Bell Bay Aluminium after coastal shipping reforms tied to unions.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2], arguing it attacks unions and worsens inequality, and cited ACOSS data showing the top 20% of earners receive five times as much as the bottom 20% and economist Joseph Stiglitz’s view that unions are a key bulwark against inequality. He supported amendments moved by the shadow minister and noted the bill was one of ten workplace deregulation bills introduced by the government.
